title: Masei: the land is shared (Numbers 35:33–34)
hookLine: bloodshed pollutes the land in which God dwells

lines: A HOUSE NOBODY WANTS TO LIVE IN.
cards: Some places hold what happened in them. People stop wanting to live in a house after something terrible happens there. A street corner gets flowers and candles for years.
Somehow, even without explaining it, people feel that ground remembers. After the cities of refuge, the Torah ends its laws about killing with two verses that say exactly that.
They aren't about the one who killed, or the family who grieves. They're about the land itself, and who else lives on it.

teach.b: Here are the verses, mostly in paraphrase.
Don't pollute the land you live in, the Torah says, because blood pollutes the land, and the land can't be cleansed of blood shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it.

Then the last line: don't defile the land you live in, where I dwell, and in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the children of Israel." Notice the turn.
It isn't only your land. Someone else lives in it too.

teach.h: THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE TENANTS.
teach.b: In Leviticus, God says it even more plainly: the land is Mine, and you are like strangers and settlers with Me. Not owners: tenants, sharing a house with its owner.
So violence isn't just a crime between two families; it stains a shared home. An early midrash says bloodshed defiles the land and causes the Divine Presence to withdraw from it.

The chapter itself, a few verses earlier, refuses any ransom for a murderer's life: no payment buys a way out. And the idea that the land itself can be harmed, and that people answer for it, has stayed in Jewish thought.
Later teachers drew from other verses a law against needless destruction, called bal tashchit, starting with not cutting down fruit trees in war.
The land is shared: with each other, with those who come after, and, the Torah says, with God.

how: These verses close the laws of homicide in Masei, read in midsummer, and Jewish law draws from related verses the principle of bal tashchit, avoiding needless destruction.

the spies: the portion of the twelve scouts

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah lets a murderer pay money instead of facing justice
the chapter says no ransom may be taken for the life of a murderer.
Leviticus says the land belongs to God
the land is Mine, and you are strangers and settlers with Me (Leviticus 25:23).
bal tashchit starts from a verse about fruit trees
not cutting down fruit trees in war (Deuteronomy 20:19).

games.q: the Torah has finished its laws about killing. what's its very last word on the subject?
o: the families must settle it themselves.
don't defile the land, for God dwells in it.
the killer must pay a fine.
games.why: it ends with the land: blood pollutes it, and God dwells in the midst of it. the harm reaches a shared home.

practice: Picture a small patch of ground in your life: a yard, a window box, the strip of grass outside your building.

See it as a home shared with neighbors, with animals, with people who'll come after you, and, if you believe it, with God. Let one small kindness for it come to mind: litter picked up, something watered, something planted.

wordCard.voice: Masei. The portion whose laws end by saying blood pollutes the land, because God dwells in the midst of it.

orig.note: Hebrew: I dwell in the midst of it, said of the land (Numbers 35:34).

carryVoice: Your line: the land is shared. Tenants, not owners, sharing one roof. Day four hundred seventy-nine, done.
